html:
Ellis Island is a small island in New York Harbor that was the busiest immigrant inspection station of the United States from 1892 to 1954. About 12 million people passed through it.

Most arrived in the great wave of migration from Europe around 1900, fleeing poverty, hunger and persecution: Italians, Jews from the Russian Empire, Poles, Irish, Germans, Greeks, Hungarians and many others. They had crossed the Atlantic by steamship, most in crowded steerage. First- and second-class passengers were usually inspected on board, so it was the poorer travellers who were ferried to the island.

Inside, doctors watched them climb the stairs to the great hall, looking for signs of illness, and inspectors asked questions about money, work and plans. Most were through in a few hours. Only about two in every hundred were sent back, mostly for disease or because they seemed likely to need public support. The island sat in sight of the Statue of Liberty, dedicated in 1886.

The flow slowed with the First World War, then almost stopped after laws in 1921 and 1924 set quotas that favoured northern Europeans and shut out most others. Earlier, the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 had already barred Chinese workers, and Asians entering on the west coast went through Angel Island in San Francisco. Ellis Island closed in 1954 and is now a museum of immigration. By one estimate, two in five Americans have an ancestor who came through it.
sum: Ellis Island is a small island in New York Harbor that was the busiest immigrant inspection station of the United States from 1892 to 1954. About 12 million people passed through it.
